title: JP Morgan cites reforms for Nigeria expansion - Punch Newspapers
content:
JPMorgan Chase & Co has linked its planned expansion in Nigeria to the impact of economic reforms and the quality of banking regulation, as the United States lender moves closer to securing a merchant banking licence from the Central Bank of Nigeria. The bank has deposited N50bn, equivalent to about $38m, with the CBN as part of the requirements for its licence application, according to a Bloomberg report on Tuesday. The Managing Director of JPMorgan West Africa, Dapo Olagunju, said the country’s reform programme and regulatory framework were key considerations behind the lender’s decision to deepen its presence in the market. “The level of reforms and the impact of the reforms is why we are expanding in Nigeria. We are also very impressed with the quality of banking regulations at the central bank,” Olagunju said. The bank is targeting approval by December 2026 or early 2027, although the final decision rests with the CBN. People familiar with the application process told Bloomberg that the N50bn deposit was one of the final regulatory requirements for approval. They requested anonymity because the process is private. The proposed licence would enable the lender to expand beyond its existing representative office in Lagos and offer a broader range of services to Nigerian businesses and institutions, subject to the terms of the approval. JPMorgan has operated in Nigeria primarily through its representative office, advising governments and companies on Eurobond issuances and other financial transactions. A merchant banking licence would provide a platform for it to deepen its involvement in corporate finance, lending and trade-related services. The N50bn deposit represents a significant step towards establishing a licensed banking operation in the country. However, it does not guarantee approval, and the bank cannot commence the proposed operations solely on the basis of the payment. The expansion plan comes as international financial institutions seek opportunities in African markets, where businesses and governments require financing, investment banking services and support for cross-border trade. Nigeria’s large economy and corporate sector make it an important market for lenders seeking to expand their African operations. JPMorgan’s proposed entry would strengthen its capacity to serve local companies and institutions directly, depending on the scope of the licence granted. The bank has also been strengthening its investment banking leadership across the continent. It appointed Edward Bell to lead investment banking in sub-Saharan Africa, while Sailepu Montet was named head of its Kenya office and Michael Ahonzo Avou was appointed to oversee operations in Ivory Coast. The appointments form part of its broader efforts to build capacity in key African markets. All rights reserved. title: JPMorgan Identifies 40 Stocks With a Surprising Edge - TradingView
content: JPMorgan JPM has identified 40 stocks it believes are particularly well positioned for a higher-interest-rate environment, as investors increasingly consider the possibility that borrowing costs stay elevated for longer. The basket draws on recommendations from JPMorgan's equity analysts and focuses on businesses with characteristics that can either benefit from higher rates or absorb them better than more leveraged peers. The group includes financial institutions, cash-rich consumer companies, oil producers, auto-parts retailers, waste-management businesses and select technology names, according to Seeking Alpha. Financial companies can benefit when higher rates lift interest income on loans, securities and client balances faster than funding costs increase. JPMorgan itself recently said it remains asset-sensitive and expects part of its projected 2027 net-interest-income growth to come from a higher yield curve. JPMorgan is also favoring companies that can fund growth internally and do not rely heavily on refinancing debt at higher rates. That matters because businesses with large cash balances and low leverage face much less pressure when the cost of capital rises. The bank also highlighted companies with differentiated or resilient consumer demand, which can help protect revenue even when higher borrowing costs slow the broader economy. The strategy comes as higher rates remain a central market risk. JPMorgan executives have acknowledged that persistently high real rates would eventually slow economic activity and could pressure consumers, even though household balance sheets and spending have remained relatively resilient so far. I think the important part of JPMorgan's basket is that it is not simply telling investors to hide from higher rates. It is looking for businesses where the rate environment can actually become an advantage. For banks and other asset-sensitive financial firms, that can mean stronger interest income. For cash-rich companies, it means earning more on liquidity while avoiding expensive refinancing. And for businesses with strong customer demand, pricing power can provide another layer of protection. For investors, the key things to watch are net interest income, debt maturity schedules, free cash flow, consumer resilience and whether the Fed keeps rates elevated into 2027. Higher rates are usually treated as a broad market headwind. JPMorgan's point is that for the right companies, they can also create winners. Select market data provided by ICE Data Services. title: J.P. Morgan Names Former Merrill Manager to Lead Southeast Market - AdvisorHub
content: Over a year after leaving thundering herd as part of a reorganization, former Merrill Lynch Private Wealth regional leader Linda A. Patel has returned to management at J.P. Morgan Advisors, the New York bank’s traditional brokerage unit. Linda A. Patel, who previously oversaw Merrill’s ultra-high net worth brokers in Texas, joined J.P. Morgan Advisors as head of its Southeast territory based in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, according to an announcement on Tuesday. Patel oversees around 80 advisors in Palm Beach Gardens, Palm Beach, Boca Raton, Miami and Atlanta, according to the announcement. She reports to J.P. Morgan Advisors Head Mollie Colavita and succeeds Janet Sweeney, a 40-year industry veteran who retired earlier this year. Sweeny had joined J.P. Morgan through its 2023 acquisition of First Republic Bank’s wealth unit. The appointment comes a little over a week after two of J.P. Morgan’s largest teams, who had generated $130 million in combined revenue from $18.6 billion in assets, left to launch RIA Latigo Peak Partners based in Palm Beach Gardens. “The Southeast continues to attract individuals, families and businesses with increasingly complex financial needs – creating significant opportunity for us to build on our strength in the region and grow alongside our clients,” Colavita said in a statement. Patel was one of two Merrill Private Wealth leaders who left in July 2025 as the firm consolidated six regions to four. She had led its Texas region since 2018 after overseeing offices in Thousand Oaks, California. Patel started her career at UBS’s PaineWebber predecessor in 1998 and joined Merrill through a predecessor later that year, according to BrokerCheck. She did not respond to a request for comment sent through social media. J.P. Morgan Advisors has around 600 advisors and remains a small fraction of JPMorgan Chase & Co.’s wealth business. Colavita, a former senior executive at Merrill Private Wealth, took over the top job at J.P. Morgan Advisors in October 2025 following the retirement of Phil Sieg, who was once head of Merrill Private Wealth. A Merrill spokesperson did not immediately return a request for comment. The name carries both aspiration and promise, and, for more than five decades, the San Francisco nonprofit it describes has worked to make that promise real for thousands of older adults across the Bay Area. In 1971, a group of community members in San Francisco’s Chinatown North Beach neighborhood asked a deceptively simple question: Why should a person spend the final years of their life in a nursing home, far from the streets they walked, the food they loved and the language they spoke? Their answer: They shouldn’t. And that’s how On Lok was founded. For too many Americans, aging with dignity remains harder than it should be: Healthcare is fragmented, costs are rising and families navigate a maze of providers and social services. On Lok was built to meet that need. Problem: On Lok needed to open two new 23,000-square-foot centers in Union City and South San Jose simultaneously, while continuing to serve thousands of seniors across its existing programs, with complex multi-year financing needs that exceeded typical nonprofit banking. As On Lok proved the model locally, its leaders wanted to test whether it could work beyond San Francisco. They took the concept to the federal government as a demonstration and established a unique way to finance the program through Medicare and Medicaid to deliver the full range of services seniors need to stay in their communities. With grant support, On Lok worked with six organizations in six states to teach the approach and show it could deliver quality care beyond a single city or population. That proof helped pave the way for a permanent funding framework within Medicare regulations. Today, PACE operates in 33 states and the District of Columbia, serving more than 100,000 people. It’s not easy to age and On Lok has been thinking about what our community members need as they age for 55 years.” On Lok’s services span a continuum of aging: active seniors come to senior centers for exercise, art, computer labs and communal meals; those with more complex needs receive care management and help navigating insurance and housing; and for seniors whose chronic conditions make daily life genuinely difficult, the PACE program provides fully integrated medical and social support that keeps them in the community rather than in institutional care. “On Lok’s mission is the voice of aging,” said Nicole Torres, COO and a 24-year member of the organization. Torres began her career as a nurse—starting in pediatrics at Lucile Packard at Stanford—before shifting into older-adult care and joining On Lok as a home care nurse. “We are serving people who are yearning to age as they want to age. We are also serving communities that need us, who are vulnerable, who are unheard.” Marie, a pianist and PACE participant at the On Lok 30th Street Center, came to On Lok after breaking her femur during the pandemic. Today she plays piano for fellow participants several times a week. “I kept hoping I could play music for people again. The dream came true,” Marie said. She is also grateful for the healthcare support: “It’s a lifesaver for me.” Jeffrey, a 66-year-old former cable linesman and self-taught artist at the On Lok PACE South San Jose Center, has had his drawings celebrated by staff and shared with other participants. “The medical support here is impressive,” he said. “I thought I was at the end of my rope. On Lok takes good care of me.” On Lok’s reach is deeply local: It employs physicians, nurses, social workers, therapists, drivers and nutritionists, and contracts with local small businesses and community providers. Its impact extends far beyond its walls, strengthening families, caregivers and the community institutions that make neighborhoods work. Employees also volunteer directly at On Lok, playing bingo with participants and tending the center’s garden. On Lok’s story is, at its core, a story about generations. The organization is now serving the children and grandchildren of the first seniors it cared for in 1971. That generational continuity is both a measure of past success and a mandate for what comes next. “We’re already serving generations of families,” Li said. “There are grandkids who always would come and know On Lok because they visited their grandparent here or their parent here.” Torres looks ahead with clarity. “The next 55 years look bright. title: J.P. Morgan’s Nigeria presence signals investor confidence in Tinubu’s reforms – NRS - Businessday NG
content:
The growing presence of global financial institution J.P. Morgan in Nigeria signals renewed international investor confidence in the country’s  economicNigerian Banking Launch The growing presence of global financial institution J.P. Morgan in Nigeria signals renewed international investor confidence in the country’s economic reforms, the Nigeria Revenue Service (NRS) has said, as the Federal Government seeks to strengthen fiscal stability and attract long-term foreign capital. Zacch Adedeji, executive chairman of the NRS, stated this on Monday when he received Adedapo Olagunju, the newly appointed managing director of J.P. Morgan Nigeria, during a courtesy visit to the service’s headquarters in Abuja. Adedeji said the confidence of international financial institutions reflected the credibility, stability and predictability that President Bola Tinubu’s economic reforms and fiscal policies were seeking to establish. He noted that a transparent, efficient and predictable fiscal environment remained critical to attracting global capital, strengthening institutional partnerships and positioning Nigeria as a competitive investment destination. According to him, the growing interest of major international financial institutions reinforces the importance of sustaining reforms that improve the  business environment and provide investors with greater certainty in making long-term investment decisions. Adedeji added that as the reforms continue to take shape, the confidence shown by institutions such as J.P. Morgan sends a signal that Nigeria is working to establish stronger foundations for sustainable economic growth and investment. The meeting comes against the backdrop of far-reaching economic changes introduced by the Tinubu administration since May 2023, including the removal of the petrol subsidy and the unification of the foreign exchange market. The reforms were designed to reduce pressure on public finances, improve the functioning of the foreign exchange market and address longstanding distortions in the  economy. However, they have also contributed to higher living costs and increased operating expenses for businesses, placing pressure on households and the private sector. For investors, the effectiveness of these policy changes will depend not only on the reforms themselves but also on their consistent implementation, macroeconomic stability, access to foreign exchange and the ability of businesses to plan with greater certainty. Fiscal policy and revenue administration are central to this process. The Federal Government needs stronger and more predictable revenue mobilisation to finance public services, infrastructure and other development priorities while reducing excessive dependence on borrowing. The NRS, which is responsible for administering federal taxes and driving improvements in revenue collection, occupies a strategic position in the government’s efforts to strengthen public finances. Greater efficiency, transparency and predictability in tax administration can help improve compliance, broaden the revenue base and build confidence among businesses operating in Nigeria. For international financial institutions, a more predictable fiscal environment can also support assessments of investment risks, financing opportunities and the broader outlook for the Nigerian economy. J.P. Morgan is a major international financial services institution with operations spanning investment banking, markets, payments and asset management. Its engagement with Nigerian authorities is therefore significant in the context of the country’s efforts to maintain links with global financial markets and attract international capital. However, the presence or engagement of a global financial institution does not, on its own, establish the scale of new investment commitments or guarantee improved economic outcomes. The broader significance will depend on whether confidence translates into increased capital flows, expanded business activity and improved access to financing for the Nigerian economy. Adedeji said the confidence of leading global financial institutions reinforced the importance of continuing reforms aimed at creating a stable and transparent economic environment. He maintained that Nigeria was building the foundations for sustainable growth and long-term investment as the reforms progressed. The NRS did not disclose specific investment commitments arising from the meeting or indicate whether the engagement would lead to new financing arrangements between J.P. Morgan and the Nigerian government. Nevertheless, the engagement highlights the importance of credible fiscal institutions and consistent economic policies in Nigeria’s efforts to strengthen investor confidence, improve revenue performance and secure a more sustainable path to  economic growth. title: HSBC launches RedCoin, JP Morgan and ADB expand India working-capital support - The Asian Banker
content: Transaction Finance Weekly: Hong Kong stablecoins gain a major bank’s payment network, while recipient verification and shared settlement arrangements advance across Asia. Hong Kong’s regulated stablecoin market is developing across consumer payments, investment subscriptions and corporate transactions. HSBC’s RedCoin launch adds a major bank’s existing payment network to that expansion, bringing distribution and practical uses into focus. Elsewhere, JP Morgan and ADB expanded working-capital risk sharing in India, while TerraPay integrated recipient verification with Kinexys Liink to address cross-border payment errors. Ripple expanded its treasury platform, and Malaysia and Thailand joined BLOOM’s work on common arrangements for digital-money settlement. HSBC launched its Hong Kong dollar-denominated stablecoin, RedCoin, on 23 October through PayMe, with wallet activation rolling out to more than 3.3 million users and payments supported at more than 100,000 merchants. The launch implements the initial peer-to-peer and merchant-payment phase outlined on 30 September. HSBC plans to add mobile banking wallet functionality and tokenised investment subscriptions later this year, including a planned share class of its HKD money market fund, with corporate and institutional applications also planned. RedCoin initially operates within HSBC-controlled infrastructure, with wider blockchain connectivity dependent on further regulatory approval. It runs on a private, permissioned blockchain operated by HSBC; public-chain connectivity would require HKMA approval. RedCoin is backed by segregated HKD reserve assets and redeemable at par, but pays no interest and is not covered by Hong Kong’s Deposit Protection Scheme. Rival Anchorpoint began rolling out HKDAP in August through distributors serving institutional, corporate and professional-investor markets. JP Morgan Payments and the Asian Development Bank announced on 22 October an expanded collaboration to broaden access to working capital for businesses across India through a risk-sharing framework. The arrangement covers trade and working-capital finance across supply chains, including financing for manufacturers, buyers and suppliers. Target sectors include food, pharmaceuticals, electric vehicles and renewable energy. The collaboration builds on a longstanding relationship. In 2017, ADB and JP Morgan introduced a funded risk-sharing product expected to support more than $100 million in trade across developing Asia. The latest announcement extends their cooperation to Indian corporates and their supply chains. ADB’s guarantee transfers part of the credit risk on eligible exposures, potentially enabling JP Morgan to finance transactions that would otherwise be constrained by its credit limits or risk appetite. Ripple launched new capabilities for Ripple Treasury on 26 October, connecting cash positioning, forecasting, reconciliation, liquidity management and payments. The platform includes 24/7 Returns, which allows eligible corporate customers to generate returns on qualifying digital assets held in a Ripple wallet, including Ripple’s dollar-backed stablecoin RLUSD, subject to programme requirements. Ripple says customers can put eligible assets to work outside traditional banking hours without managing the underlying digital-asset transactions themselves. The announcement builds on Ripple’s $1 billion GTreasury acquisition, announced in October 2025, and September’s expansion of GSmart’s treasury AI capabilities. The announcement does not specify the underlying return-generating strategy, which corporate treasury teams would need to assess alongside access to liquidity and investment policies. The Monetary Authority of Singapore announced on 23 October that Bank Negara Malaysia and the Bank of Thailand had joined BLOOM as policymaker members. Participants are developing common arrangements for accepting, exchanging and settling tokenised deposits and regulated stablecoins across jurisdictions, including contractual arrangements, identity verification and sanctions controls. MAS says this could reduce the separate agreements and integrations financial institutions need for each counterparty or market. Under BLOOM, Ripple announced a pilot with trade finance technology provider Unloq in March using RLUSD to release trade payments when predefined conditions, such as shipment verification, are met. Visa announced a pilot with Nium in August, also under BLOOM, to explore stablecoin settlement across weekends and public holidays. These applications depend on receiving institutions being able to recognise, accept and settle the digital money under their own regulatory and operating requirements. BLOOM’s common arrangements seek to address those requirements across jurisdictions. TerraPay announced on 22 October that it had integrated its Verify payee-verification service with JP Morgan’s Kinexys Liink Confirm application. The integration allows banks and non-bank financial institutions connected to Liink, as well as TerraPay Verify clients, to validate recipient bank-account and digital-wallet details across global markets before initiating payments. The service targets payment failures caused by inaccurate beneficiary information, adding TerraPay’s verification coverage to Confirm’s existing account-validation capabilities. Checking recipient details before funds move can reduce rejected payments and the manual work needed to investigate and resubmit them. The announcement establishes expanded verification access, but provides no measured reduction in payment failures or fraud. Visa announced enhanced commercial payment capabilities on 21 October, including supplier-spend analytics, virtual-card fraud controls and a live invoice-payment pilot with BILL and Billtrust first announced the previous day. In the pilot, an authorised AI agent initiates and completes approved invoice payments through supplier portals using tokenised credentials and buyer-defined controls. Visa said end-to-end transactions were being processed with participating BILL customers and Billtrust suppliers. The pilot extends Visa’s Trusted Agent Protocol, introduced with partners in October 2025, into business invoice payments across buyer and supplier platforms. Billtrust authenticates the agent accessing the supplier portal, allowing it to complete an approved payment without shared supplier login credentials. The buyer retains payment approval authority while the agent carries out the portal interaction. Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation (SMBC) and Ant International signed a memorandum of understanding on 26 October to collaborate on cross-border payments and transaction flows involving Japan, Singapore and Southeast Asia. SMBC will support Ant International’s Alipay+, Antom and WorldFirst businesses with payments and treasury management. The parties will also explore integrating Ant’s Whale RTP platform with SMBC’s digital payment and asset solutions to support intercompany treasury and global liquidity management. Ant has already pursued related treasury initiatives with other banks, including DBS’s treasury-token pilot and Standard Chartered’s HKD blockchain test settlement. On 7 October, OCBC announced a tokenised-deposit service enabling Ant to manage liquidity between Singapore and Malaysia around the clock. SMBC’s agreement adds another potential banking connection to that network, although its proposed technical integration remains exploratory. Ping An Digital Bank launched Receivables Financing and Invoice Financing on 21 October for Hong Kong importers and exporters, offering revolving facilities of up to HKD 50 million ($6.4 million). Exporters can obtain advances against outstanding receivables using commercial invoices and bills of lading, while importers can have approved financing paid directly to suppliers, with repayment terms of three to six months. The bank says digital drawdowns can provide funds in as little as one business day. The products extend an offering that includes purchase-order financing and cross-border e-commerce revolving loans. They address different points in the trade cash cycle: exporters obtain liquidity while awaiting customer payments, while importers finance supplier payments before generating sales proceeds. For its existing Trade-Connect loans, the bank also uses consenting Tradelink customers’ trade-declaration data to support credit assessment. The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development renewed its Regional Trade Facilitation Programme on 21 October, with a maximum outstanding amount of EUR 4.5 billion ($5.1 billion). The programme provides guarantees covering payment risk on trade-finance instruments issued by participating banks and factors, as well as revolving cash advances that allow participating institutions to finance exporters and importers. The programme began in 1999 and was previously renewed in February 2025. At the end of 2025, more than 140 banks and factoring companies in 27 EBRD countries of operation were accredited, while more than 800 banks in 82 countries participated as confirming banks. The renewal maintains this established channel connecting local trade lenders with international confirming institutions. The African Development Bank approved a EUR 40 million ($44.9 million) facility for AFG Bank Cameroon on 21 October, comprising a EUR 30 million ($33.7 million) trade-finance credit line over 3.5 years and a EUR 10 million ($11.2 million) transaction guarantee facility over five years. The guarantee can provide up to 100% coverage to confirming banks for eligible letters of credit and similar trade-finance instruments issued by AFG Bank Cameroon. Half of the credit line is earmarked for SMEs, with 30% of that SME allocation directed to women- or youth-owned enterprises. The credit line funds AFG’s trade lending, while the guarantee covers eligible payment risk faced by confirming banks. Providing liquidity to the issuing bank alone does not remove that risk. The facility extends an approach AfDB has also used with Cameroon’s CCA-Bank, whose earlier package combined a trade credit line with a transaction guarantee. © Copyright 2026, The Asian Banker. It's the first time the report has put a range on Bitcoin's returns, and it comes with a handful of heavy caveats. Although the figures it calculated are unlikely to prove true in 2036, the drivers for those results are hard to argue against, and it's my view that JPMorgan Chase is directionally correct. Here's why. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » The JPMorgan Chase report is largely about the investing implications of the macroeconomic conditions facing the world during the coming years, touching on everything from inflation to global warming and, of course, Bitcoin. It expects artificial-intelligence-driven productivity gains to push the U.S. economy's real growth rate to 2.1% annually, with inflation averaging 2.4% in the same period. It also raised its expected annual return for large companies, such as those in the S&P 500 index, from 6.7% to 7.5%, citing strong profit margins. But it contends that Bitcoin will be buoyed by three different factors that will offer better performance than this. The most important driver, with a 65% weight in the calculation, is Bitcoin's slowing supply growth relative to global money growth. The second-most-important factor, with a weight of 30%, is Bitcoin's inclusion in portfolios alongside allocations to other scarce store-of-value assets, such as gold. The last driver is the weakest: the coin's increasing network activity. The bank's estimated growth rate for its base case implies that Bitcoin would be priced at about $211,130 by 2036. Its bear case, which calls for an 11.2% annual loss, implies a price of about $24,817, roughly 70% below its $81,300 level as of Oct. 26. The bull case would see it grow by 16.6% annually. But no matter which of those scenarios plays out, the bank expects the coin's volatility to be 55%, based on historical data. Overall, JPMorgan Chase's projections for Bitcoin's price growth are on the bearish side compared to Bitcoin's history, but they look reasonable. The coin has a 10-year compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 63%. The supply model is difficult to dispute; Bitcoin's next halving, when the number of new coins miners earn per block is halved, is expected sometime in April 2028. The U.S. M2, one gauge of the broad money supply, grew by 5.7% in the year through August 2026. The bank doubts that a currency-debasement scare will spark a rush into crypto, but its model doe assumes a modest shift. Its projected inflation during the next decade is significantly lower than September 2026's 3.7% annual pace, which means that if inflation remains elevated, the importance of Bitcoin as a potential hedge against it could drive its performance toward the bull case. Still, the bank calls the coin "a speculative asset and a hedge against monetary easing." It says volatility has declined, but unstable correlations make Bitcoin premature as a diversifier. Though JPMorgan Chase still doesn't recommend buying Bitcoin, it probably makes sense to own at least a little to gain exposure to its upside in the bank's base case, and perhaps a bit more upside if the bull case plays out. title: JP Morgan Sees 8% Return in U.S. Bonds as Real Yields Hit 25-Year High - Seoul Economic Daily
content:
Bonds Over Stocks? The Opportunity JP Morgan Is Watching
Real Yields at 3%, Highest Since 2002
U.S. Bonds Seen Returning 8% Over 12 Months U.S. Treasury yields have climbed to their highest levels in more than two decades, drawing attention to bonds as an investment. J.P. Morgan Asset Management said real yields have reached a roughly 25-year peak and that investors could earn returns of as much as 8% over the next 12 months. Bob Michele, global head of fixed income at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, told a press briefing in Singapore that "everyone senses there is a once-in-a-generation yield in the bond market" and that "yield is everywhere," according to Reuters on the 27th. Michele said that combining interest income with price gains, U.S. bond investments could deliver returns of 7% to 8% over the coming 12 months. He also suggested that the U.S. policy rate and the Treasury yield curve could both converge around 4.5%. "Typically at the end of a rate-hiking cycle the yield curve flattens, and from current levels there is plenty of room for yields to move further," he said. His central argument rested on the level of real yields. "When Treasury yields first passed 5% a few weeks ago, the buy signal for us was that the U.S. real yield had reached 3%," Michele said. "The last time we saw these levels was 2002. That is nearly 25 years, so it is a buying opportunity." 10-Year Yield at 5.35%, With Further Hikes a Wild Card U.S. Treasury yields have surged recently as inflation concerns combined with the Federal Reserve's tightening stance. The 10-year yield broke above 5% on the 14th of last month for the first time since October 2023, and on the 7th of this month exceeded 5.35%, its highest level since 2002. The moves are attributed to rising inflation concerns from higher international oil prices tied to the war in Iran, as well as the Fed's quarter-percentage-point increase last month that lifted the policy rate to 3.75% to 4.0%. The 10-year yield eased to around 4.99% on the 27th, and developed-market government bond markets that had recently sold off also showed signs of a rebound. Markets expect the Fed to hold its benchmark rate steady at the Federal Open Market Committee meeting that concludes on the 28th. Beyond U.S. Treasuries, Japanese and Australian government bonds, investment-grade corporate debt and emerging-market sovereign bonds were also cited as promising. "Capital expenditure cycles are continuing worldwide, so the likelihood of a recession is very low," Michele said. "Whenever credit spreads — the gap between government and corporate bond yields — widen, you should buy." A risk remains that inflation could become unsettled again, forcing the Fed to raise its policy rate well above 4.5%. Original reporting by Kang Ji-won for Seoul Economic Daily. title: China tax crackdown hasn't hurt asset management flow - JP Morgan AM - The Standard (HK)
content: Beijing's drive to tax offshore income, which is prompting some wealthy Chinese to sell assets abroad, has not hit investor flows into J.P. Morgan's asset management division in Asia, according to its Singapore, Southeast Asia and India head. "You may have things that happen that will affect those flows. But my general view is these are things that just may be a bump in the road, but the road continues," said Ayaz Ebrahim, J.P. Morgan Asset Management chief executive officer for Singapore, Southeast Asia and India, when asked about China's crackdown in an interview in Singapore. "In terms of what we're seeing in terms of flows, it hasn't really impacted at all. Our flows have been decent and they continue to be decent," he said, without offering numbers. Stockbrokers have cited the crackdown as a reason for falls in Hong Kong's equity market and in share prices for Singapore banks, which have been beneficiaries of deposits and cash flows from rich customers in China and Southeast Asia. Some of China's richest people are winding down their offshore trusts, selling shares, and even switching nationality as a deadline looms to declare income booked overseas, say wealth advisers, lawyers and others familiar with the matter. Ebrahim, who has nearly four decades in markets, said he asset manager was "clearly focusing" on Asia's wealth boom. "Even if China's growing at 3 percent – it's creating a lot of money still.. I think this trend is here to stay. Definitely," he said. He said the asset manager, which has US$4.6 trillion in assets under management according to its website, had recently opened a two-person trading desk in Singapore and that by the first quarter of next year, headcount would have expanded by 20 percent to 25 percent over the years since he moved to Singapore in April 2024.

It's another sign of the growing acceptance of cryptocurrency. CEO Jamie Dimon previously called Bitcoin a fraud, and as recently as 2025, he said he didn't see its value. Its bear case is -11.2%, and its bull case is about 16.5%. For perspective, JPMorgan forecasts annualized returns of 7.5% for U.S. large-cap stocks, 7.7% for small-cap stocks, 5.5% for gold, and 5.6% to 6.6% for U.S. bonds. Real estate investment trusts (REITs) came in at 8.2%. If JPMorgan's base cases are accurate, $100 invested in Bitcoin would grow to $259 over the next 10 years. The same amount invested in large caps would grow to $206. The press release for JPMorgan's report specifically noted that Bitcoin isn't included as an allocation. The bank also hasn't yet included Bitcoin in its main covariance matrices, the models it uses to determine how much of an asset belongs in a portfolio. JPMorgan laid out two obstacles to Bitcoin portfolio use: volatility and unstable correlations with other assets. Cryptocurrency is known for its volatility, and in Bitcoin's case, JPMorgan assumes 55% annualized volatility, compared to 18% for U.S. large caps and 17.2% for gold. This volatility is why there's such a large gap between the bull and bear cases for Bitcoin. In the bear case, where Bitcoin loses 11.2% per year, you'd end up with roughly 30% of your money after 10 years. Bitcoin's unstable correlations with other assets make it difficult to allocate in a portfolio. A small position in Bitcoin is worth considering if you have a high tolerance for risk and volatility. The cryptocurrency has historically outperformed stocks by a wide margin during its bull markets, with the trade-off that it suffers much greater losses during bear markets. As of Oct. 26, with Bitcoin trading about 36% below the all-time high it set in October 2025, investors can buy in well below its peak. It's not a must-have, though -- investing in stocks is the far more proven option, and you don't need Bitcoin to get market-beating returns. The bank earned $15.3 billion, or $5.57 a share, in the third quarter, though the results fell short of Wall Street's estimates in a rare miss, CNBC reported. Yet the more telling part of the report sat beneath the profit. Jamie Dimon used it to flag a short list of risks building under a still-strong economy. In an interview days later, he described the U.S. economy as booming, while warning that inflationary events could still push prices higher. Dimon named them in one sentence: large fiscal deficits, sticky inflation, elevated asset prices, rising interest rates, and geopolitical conditions "continue to shift under the surface," he said, according to JPMorgan's earnings release. These forces may be manageable, he added, but the bank remains prepared for a wide range of outcomes. Also read: JPMorgan CEO sends stern warning on the next credit cycle Washington's borrowing tops the list. The federal government closed fiscal 2026 with a deficit of about $1.99 trillion, which was $217 billion wider than the year before. The debt pile hasn't stopped growing either, reaching roughly $40.39 trillion on Oct. 15. Inflation and interest rates are tangled together. In May, a spike in crude oil sent the Consumer Price Index to 4.2%, its highest reading in three years, CBS News reported. The Fed answered in September by raising rates for the first time since 2023 and hinted that another hike could come this year. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said plainly that inflation had stayed too high for too long. The last two threats are harder to measure. Dimon has pointed to the remilitarization of the world and the restructuring of trade as forces that could raise prices, and inflation has risen during the Iran conflict. On the earnings call, he also acknowledged that times are good, with high asset prices and fairly low credit losses. Elevated valuations leave less room for error if any of the other four threats flare up. On the balance sheet, JPMorgan is padding its cushion. It set aside $2.7 billion for credit losses during the quarter, and $539 million of that went into reserves, mostly for wholesale loans. The bank also pulled back on share buybacks. Actual losses are still in check, though, since net charge-offs came in lower than a year ago. Dimon is also getting pickier about who gets a loan. "We are tightening up a little bit credit," he told analysts, adding that some credit terms have become a little looser. In plain terms, the bank is being more careful about the loans it makes. Other major lenders are bracing, too. Wells Fargo raised its provision for credit losses to $1.03 billion from $681 million a year earlier, Citigroup's card profits fell partly on higher loan provisioning, and Goldman Sachs' provisions in its banking and markets unit rose sharply. Broad credit damage is not evident yet, but the trend points to a cycle that's maturing. The value of leveraged loans trading at deeply distressed prices has climbed to its highest level since March 2020, according to TheStreet, and JPMorgan's strategists expect defaults on high-yield bonds and leveraged loans to rise in 2027. Technology companies make up about 39% of those distressed loans. For households, the bank's playbook starts with savings. Having an emergency fund matters more when companies feeling the squeeze may trim jobs or hold off on hiring to protect their profits. A few months of expenses tucked away can keep a rough patch from turning into a debt problem. Debt is the next place to look. The average credit card balance carries a rate of about 21.5%, according to TheStreet, so the highest-rate card is usually the one to attack first. Calling the issuer to ask for a lower rate can work, and so can a balance transfer, though those fees often land between 3% and 5%. Be cautious about new borrowing, especially loans with floating rates. The Fed's rate hike could lead to higher borrowing costs for mortgages, auto loans, and credit cards over time. Anyone planning to refinance a mortgage or roll over a car loan next year should run the numbers early. Goldman Sachs rethinks U.S. economy as interest rates stay higher Heating bills expected to jump by $1,000 in some U.S. states this winter It also pays not to lean too hard on any one hedge. Gold is the classic safe haven, yet it dropped below $4,000 an ounce on Oct. 23 and had its worst week since June. Banks spread their bets across many kinds of assets, and a family's portfolio works better when it does the same. To be clear, Dimon isn't sounding a recession alarm. He has been careful not to call a downturn. And he talks about the next credit cycle mainly as a question of whether people are ready for it. Most family budgets could stand to be asked that same question. The economy still has real strengths, and Dimon expects AI investment to support growth over the long run. But strong economies can still produce painful surprises when deficits, inflation, and rates all move in the wrong direction at once. Dimon's own message is one of preparedness. America's biggest banks are already building buffers, tightening lending standards, and watching the horizon. Households that do the same are in a better position to absorb whatever comes next. AI disruption, a deep pool of private sellers, strategic industry alignment and rich premiums for scale point to a broader deal cycle ahead. Total volume is up 26% compared with the same time period in 2025, with a 22% jump in the number of deals valued above $10 billion. J.P. Morgan expects continued momentum for a broader M&A cycle. In the latest M&A report, we explore four forces shaping the market heading into the end of the year. Infographic showing year-to-date M&A activity: 26% increase in global M&A volume versus 2025, and 22% increase in deals over $10 billion year-to-date, illustrated with teal and orange upward arrows. AI has moved from concept to execution, becoming the central driver of deals and capital formation in 2026. Hyperscalers alone are expected to spend $650 billion on capex this year, and the figure is projected to exceed $1 trillion in 2027. The gap between leaders and laggards is widening. Just 20% of organizations capture roughly 75% of AI’s economic value. Rising cybersecurity threats add urgency. The result is dealmaking that extends well beyond conventional acquisitions. Companies are securing critical inputs such as compute and power through contracts and partnerships, buying differentiated capabilities like proprietary data and talent, and repositioning exposed portfolios through carve-outs and mergers. Minority investments and partnerships lead the way: AI-driven deals made up 54% of minority stake sales in the first eight months of 2026. For subscale companies, the rising cost of competing could make a sale or merger with a scaled operator increasingly attractive, accelerating future M&A deal flow. Roughly 6 million U.S. small and midsized businesses face ownership transitions by 2035 as founders retire, putting about $5 trillion in enterprise value in play. Simultaneously, sponsors are under pressure to return capital as 2026 marks the fourth straight year of below-normal sponsor liquidity. Around 32,000 portfolio companies worth roughly $4 trillion sit unsold in the U.S., and implied holding periods have stretched to seven years versus the historical average of five. With a near-record $2 trillion in dry powder waiting to be deployed, the conditions are in place for a high-velocity M&A cycle. Sponsors are increasingly turning to structured exits including continuation vehicles, minority stake sales and net asset value financing. Infographic highlighting two figures: $1T projected hyperscaler capital expenditures in 2027, and approximately $4T of unrealized value across roughly 32,000 unsold sponsor-backed companies. Government policy is steering capital toward strategic sectors — defense, shipbuilding, bioscience, energy, semiconductors and next-generation networks — by working to lower investment risk. Shipbuilding is one such example. The White House’s February 2026 maritime action plan calls for rebuilding U.S. commercial and defense shipbuilding, including encouraging partner countries to invest in domestic shipbuilding. The plan includes financing support, tax incentives and public-private partnerships. The U.S. is encouraging partner countries to invest in domestic shipbuilding; as a result, South Korea has committed $150 billion to the effort Similarly, strategic alignment on 6G has spurred policy coordination between the U.S. and 25 other nations representing about 55% of global GDP. Members of the group have signed a pact to coordinate rollout, with standards and trials expected between 2027 and 2029. The pact aligns points of contact between nations as the 6G buildout progresses, encourages both industry and academia engagement, and aims to strengthen both supply-chain transparency and security standards on the road to commercial deployment of next-generation networks. The bigger M&A tailwind may be the knock-on effect: large strategics applying their competitive advantages to a broader opportunity set, from automakers moving into defense to industrials expanding into software. Investors continue to reward scale. Market value is concentrating in a handful of the largest companies, where increased scale and higher growth are translating into near multi-decade-high valuation premiums and multiple spreads. Valuation premiums are near all-time highs, and they show up across both company size and geography. Within the U.S., the median S&P 500 company trades at 12.6x EV/EBITDA, versus 10.4x for the small-cap S&P 600. In Europe, multiples are lower: large caps on the STOXX 200 trade at 11.0x and the FTSE 100 at 8.7x. The U.K.'s mid-cap FTSE 250 trades at just 6.6x, roughly half the S&P 500 multiple. Scaled acquirers, especially in the U.S., have a highly valued currency to pursue larger deals, including cross-border targets that look inexpensive by comparison. Meanwhile, subscale and lower-valued companies face mounting pressure to combine to close the gap. Geopolitical turmoil, higher oil prices, persistent inflation and rising interest rates may delay some transactions and widen valuation gaps. The move suggested management saw lending margins staying firmer than earlier assumed through the remainder of the year. The measure also shapes how resilient the group looks if borrowing costs fall faster than expected. By lifting guidance, management signaled that a diverse mix of loans, securities and deposits gave it room to defend margins even as the rate backdrop kept shifting beneath the sector. As the largest American bank by assets, JPMorgan Chase often sets the tone for how market observers read the rest of the sector. Coverage of Financial Stocks frequently treats the group's quarterly release as an early signal for peers posting results in the same window, from consumer-focused lenders to the big trading houses. Membership in the S&P 500 adds to that bellwether role, placing the bank among the names that broad market gauges track daily. When JPMorgan Chase posts broad strength, the read-through tends to ripple across the banking group as a whole. Against its closest American rivals, JPMorgan Chase continued to stand out on sheer scale and the breadth of its franchise. Few competitors match its reach across both Main Street banking and global capital markets, a span that lets the group capture fees across very different parts of the financial system. That diversification shaped how market participants compared the quarter with those of peers. Where some rivals lean heavily on trading or on consumer lending alone, JPMorgan Chase drew gains from several directions at once, reinforcing a market position built over many cycles. The quarter unfolded against a backdrop of shifting borrowing costs, a reviving deal pipeline and steady, if uneven, consumer spending. Each of those threads showed up in the results, from firmer advisory fees to resilient card activity among American families. Technology spending remained a defining feature of the industry, as the biggest banks poured resources into data platforms, fraud defense and digital banking. JPMorgan Chase has consistently ranked among the heaviest spenders on technology in American finance, a commitment that continued to shape how the group framed its quarter. Large American banks entered the earnings season amid a delicate balance of easing borrowing costs, resilient markets and lingering uncertainty over the pace of economic growth. Those crosscurrents can cut both ways, lifting trading desks while pressuring lending margins. JPMorgan Chase navigated that mix by leaning on its scale and diversified mix of businesses. With operations spanning consumer banking, cards, trading, advisory work and asset and wealth management, the group is structured so that strength in one area can cushion softness in another across changing conditions. Even after a strong quarter, the group flagged areas of uncertainty. A modest loss tied to securities positions weighed on the headline figure, a reminder that large balance sheets carry exposures that can swing with market pricing of bonds and other instruments. Broader headwinds persist as well, from the uncertain path of borrowing costs to questions about how long American consumers can sustain their spending. Because JPMorgan Chase posts early in the season and touches so many corners of finance, its quarter offered an early read on the health of American banking. Broad strength across trading, advisory work and consumer lending set an upbeat tone for the lenders that followed. For market participants tracking the sector, the release reinforced the group's role as a barometer of the American economy. Looking beyond the latest figures, several threads will shape how JPMorgan Chase performs across the quarters ahead. Chief among them is the path of borrowing costs, since the gap between what the bank earns on loans and pays on deposits drives a large share of its earnings. JPMorgan Chase

Capital is pouring into the sport, which has become a strategic asset class with a flourishing investment ecosystem. The 2026–2027 football season in Europe recently kicked off — and investors are hoping to score big. This is especially true as the “beautiful game” has evolved beyond a traditional spectator sport and into an attractive asset class. Major football clubs in Europe are highly sought after because they offer various opportunities for value creation, thanks to their engaged consumer base and lucrative media rights. According to Deloitte, the European football market generated a record €40.2 billion in revenue over the 2024/2025 season, crossing the €40 billion threshold for the first time. Additionally, Football Benchmark reports that the aggregate enterprise value of Europe’s top 32 football clubs has nearly tripled since 2016, significantly outpacing general inflation and traditional financial indices. Today, investors are pouring capital into European football through various avenues, from M&A to structured equity and debt financing. What are the key investment trends to watch, and how is the market maturing? The rise of multi-club ownership in European football Multi-club ownership (MCO) occurs when a single investor holds controlling or minority stakes in multiple football clubs across different leagues. It is one of the most significant investment trends in European football today, offering advantages such as: While MCO can create a conflict of interest, it is managed through strict rules — for instance, governing bodies like the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) enforce rules stating that two clubs controlled by the same owner cannot play in the same tournament. Currently, over 120 top-division football clubs in Europe — around 16% of the total — are part of an MCO network. This includes almost half of those in the “Big Five” leagues, namely: Prominent examples include RB Leipzig and FC Red Bull Salzburg (part of the Red Bull franchise), as well as Manchester City FC and Girona FC (under City Football Group). In December 2024, Everton FC became part of an MCO portfolio when it was acquired by privately held consortium The Friedkin Group, which also owns AS Roma and AS Cannes. J.P. Morgan facilitated the process, providing an initial bilateral credit facility of £130 million to fund the acquisition. Thereafter, the firm raised £350 million of debt to help refinance Everton FC’s new stadium, which opened in February 2025 — a key milestone under the club’s new ownership. The growing role of private capital and private wealth Like The Friedkin Group, private capital players are increasingly acquiring stakes in European football clubs, attracted by under-monetized commercial revenues and rising franchise valuations. More than a third of clubs in Europe’s “Big Five” leagues now have backing from private equity, venture capital or private credit firms. In August 2022, private equity firm RedBird Capital Partners purchased AC Milan from hedge fund Elliott Management for €1.2 billion, with the aim of expanding the club’s commercial presence globally. J.P. Morgan advised AC Milan on the deal, which marked the largest ever football transaction in Italy. Ultra-high-net-worth individuals are also headlining major buyouts. Take, for instance, British businessman Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s purchase of a 25% stake in Manchester United in December 2023, which was the largest ever transaction in the EMEA sporting world. J.P. Morgan advised Sir Ratcliffe on the roughly £1.25 billion deal. The firm was also instrumental in advising Italian-American businessman Rocco Commisso, the former chairman of Mediacom, in his acquisition of Serie A club ACF Fiorentina back in 2019. Transactions such as these are a testament to J.P. Morgan’s holistic sports investment banking ecosystem, with the firm’s Private Bank servicing high-net-worth individuals interested in investing in sports and the Corporate and Investment Bank facilitating the deals. “By partnering across the firm, we’re able to drive successful outcomes and deliver exceptional value for our clients,” said Eric Menell, global co-head of Sports Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. “By partnering across the firm, we’re able to drive successful outcomes and deliver exceptional value for our clients.” Global Co-Head of Sports Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan Stadium redevelopment has become a defining capital investment theme in European football. Many clubs are modernizing aging infrastructure to meet stricter UEFA standards. Some are also reimagining stadiums as mixed-use entertainment platforms that can host non-sporting events — increasing both project complexity and the scale of financing. At the same time, investor interest in sports infrastructure assets such as stadiums and arenas has increased dramatically as valuations have risen. “Part of that is due to the value of live content, which consumers are gravitating toward,” said Tim Self, head of Public Finance and Infrastructure Direct Lending at J.P. Morgan. “Also, unlike in the U.S., where new franchises are still being formed as certain leagues expand into new markets, there’s effectively a fixed supply of sports assets in Europe. As more wealth is created, there’s a lot of money chasing a limited number of top-tier sports assets — and that’s driving valuations to ever higher levels.” J.P. Morgan has structured numerous stadium financings in Europe, supporting clients with capital and arranging syndication across both loan and bond markets. The firm is the leading global arranger and agent for sports and entertainment infrastructure transactions, and has $3.5 billion in capital currently committed for stadium, arena and related infrastructure debt financings globally. A case in point is Real Madrid CF’s five-year renovation of its Santiago Bernabéu stadium, which transformed the iconic venue into a state-of-the-art entertainment hub complete with a retractable grass pitch. J.P. Morgan was deeply involved throughout the project’s lifecycle — from navigating court challenges to structuring financing terms. The firm served as sole placement agent for all four financing rounds, securing multiple ‘A’ category ratings and raising a total of €1.5 billion. In the same vein, FC Barcelona is currently refurbishing its Camp Nou stadium, with works expected to be completed by 2028. The new design is expected to increase the stadium’s capacity from 99,000 to more than 105,000 spectators, as well as add a VIP ring and a sweeping panoramic screen. J.P. Morgan spearheaded the $1.6 billion capital raise, acting as financing bank, structuring agent and placement agent. Both the Santiago Bernabéu and Camp Nou are slated to host matches during the 2030 FIFA World Cup, showcasing the outcomes of these transactions on a global stage. “As more wealth is created, there’s a lot of money chasing a limited number of top-tier sports assets — and that’s driving valuations to ever higher levels.” Head of Public Finance and Infrastructure Direct Lending, J.P. Morgan From blockbuster deals to behind-the-scenes transactions While mega-deals continue to dominate headlines, investors are also supporting European football clubs behind the scenes. “Football clubs today sit on a broad range of valuable but often illiquid assets,” said Taoufik Bounhar, global head of Credit Solutions Trading at J.P. Morgan. “Our Global Credit Solutions Trading team works alongside our Banking, Public Finance and Private Bank partners to deliver bespoke financing and liquidity solutions, helping clubs and owners unlock value from player transfer-related cash flows, as well as media, sponsorship and other contractual receivables. We also offer selected opportunities that we underwrite to our Alternative Credit investors — either through outright participation or synthetic risk-transfer structures — creating efficient capital solutions for clubs while providing investors access to differentiated credit investment opportunities.” In addition, J.P. Morgan offers European football clubs other solutions like debt structuring. For instance, following Chelsea FC’s takeover in 2022, J.P. Morgan structured an £800 million debt facility for the club’s new owners, investment consortium BlueCo. The package included a £500 million term loan dedicated to infrastructure and operational investments, and a £300 million revolving credit facility for working capital. More recently, Sporting Clube de Portugal (also known as Sporting Lisbon) teamed up with J.P. Morgan in October 2025 to raise €225 million in debt, which was secured via a private placement of bonds. The funds will be used to refinance the club’s existing loans and support day-to-day operations. “Our Global Credit Solutions Trading team works alongside our Banking, Public Finance and Private Bank partners to deliver bespoke financing and liquidity solutions, helping clubs and owners unlock value from player transfer-related cash flows, as well as media, sponsorship and other contractual receivables.” Global Head of Credit Solutions Trading, J.P. Morgan. Capital continues to pour into European football: according to Deloitte, club revenues are expected to hit a new record of €44 billion for the 2025/2026 season. However, the market is gradually maturing: alongside headline takeovers, a steady pipeline of refinancings and private placements is helping to create a deeper, more resilient investment ecosystem. J.P. Morgan has established an extensive track record across the full spectrum of European football finance, supporting some of the continent’s most prominent clubs — and this momentum looks set to continue. “There is an influx of new investors chasing sports and sports-related businesses as the market expands,” said Gian Piero Sammartano, global co-head of Sports Investment Banking at J.P. Morgan. “To this end, J.P. Morgan is committed to delivering holistic advisory and financing solutions to both current and prospective sports clients across the globe.” “J.P. Morgan is committed to delivering holistic advisory and financing solutions to both current and prospective sports clients across the globe.” Global Co-Head of Sports Investment Banking, J.P. Morgan Adjust your filter selections to find what you’re looking for FOR INSTITUTIONAL & PROFESSIONAL CLIENTS ONLY – NOT INTENDED FOR RETAIL CUSTOMER USE This material has been prepared by J.P. Morgan Sales and Trading personnel and is not the product of J.P. Morgan’s Research Department. Football clubs are finding resourceful ways to turn present assets into upfront liquidity as competition, tighter lending and shifting balance sheet regulations reshape the market. Growing global attraction to football has raised enterprise valuations of clubs to the highest levels in history. A recent report on the top 32 European clubs placed the total value at €72.6 billion, a 12% increase over 2025 and almost three times the level recorded when statistics were first aggregated in 2016.1 With those lofty valuations comes an increased level of competition, and an increasing concentration of value among the legacy clubs. In the English Premier League (EPL) alone, clubs paid a record €3.6 billion in transfer fees during the 2025 summer transfer window, according to data from transfermarkt.com.2 These fees are often settled through installments over several years, creating forecastable future cash inflows that can be converted into upfront funding from banks and private lenders. Monetizing these contractual receivables can provide clubs with a lower-cost way to raise working capital — financing that is increasingly necessary as player valuations rise and new regulations such as the EPL’s Profit and Sustainability Rules (PSR) cap allowable losses over a rolling multiyear period to promote financial stability. “European Football has evolved into an established institutional investment market, with a growing range of opportunities across the capital structure” says Taoufik Bounhar, global head of Credit Solutions Trading at J.P. Morgan. “Leading clubs have built globally recognized brands with significant commercial value. For alternative credit investors, that can translate into opportunities backed by newly contracted revenue streams that can be monetized or financed.” To harness this intrinsic brand value, raise working capital and remain competitive with peers, clubs are seeking innovative financing solutions to monetize their receivables into near-term liquidity. “We structure financing and asset monetization solutions around the clubs’ contractual cash flows, enabling them to accelerate liquidity, optimize their funding costs and manage balance-sheet counterparty exposures,” said Bounhar. Importantly, this financing format strives to be less about lending against team performance and more about converting unconditional cash flows into upfront liquidity. J.P. Morgan assesses the underlying receivables, obligor credit quality, contractual enforceability and expected payment profile before structuring and pricing the transactions. The bank then may retain and risk-manage the exposure or distribute it to institutional investors through an outright assignment, sub-participation or synthetic risk-transfer. The club can assess whether receiving cash up front would enable them to pursue more opportunities than simply collecting the installments as they come due. By receiving immediate liquidity, the club can deploy the proceeds toward capex or player spending. “We structure financing and asset monetization solutions around the clubs’ contractual cash flows, enabling them to accelerate liquidity, optimize their funding costs and manage balance-sheet counterparty exposures” Global Head of Credit Solutions Trading, J.P. Morgan. Three financing strategies: Transfer receivables, contracts and media rights monetization There are three primary ways clubs are monetizing their rosters, contracts and popularity: In this arrangement, lenders purchase the receivables outright from a selling club, providing upfront proceeds at terms that are close to face value rather than face-value installments over time. The purchase price is discounted at a rate tied to the buying club’s creditworthiness, the payment schedule and the available contractual and statutory protections. Across the seven major leagues, more than $1 billion in player transfer receivables have been transacted through J.P. Morgan over the past five years. In this arrangement, lenders monetize the receivables owed to a club under its commercial agreements, namely sponsorship, naming rights and kit supply agreements, helping the club raise liquidity. Credit assessment focuses on payment obligations, counterparty creditworthiness, remaining contract tenor, termination provisions and enforceability. Where contractual cash flows are sufficiently robust, the financing may be provided more efficiently than unsecured, club-level borrowing. In this arrangement, clients receive cash due from broadcaster deals, leveraging the credit quality of the broadcasters and high visibility of multi-year broadcasting cycles. Media rights financing is structured against identifiable broadcasting distributions or contracted payment entitlements. Advance rates, tenor and pricing depend on the certainty of those cash flows, the creditworthiness of the paying counterparty and exposure to sporting contingencies, including relegation. Two deals led by J.P. Morgan saw the monetization of more than €200 million worth of media rights due from broadcasters to a high-profile Spanish La Liga football club and to a European premier division league. “We expect institutional investment in women’s football to deepen as the sport’s commercial revenues, sponsorship base and media distribution develop. The opportunity is substantial, and investment structures will reflect the sector’s stage of development and revenue visibility,” said Bounhar. title: Rockefeller Adds J.P. Morgan Team in Houston - Wealth Management
content: Rockefeller Capital Management has expanded its Global Family Office division, bringing on a seven-member Houston team led by Chris Sheets and Forrest Green from J.P. Morgan. Rockefeller Capital Management has added a Houston-based team of advisors from J.P. Morgan to its Global Family Office division. The team, led by managing directors Chris Sheets and Forrest Green, previously managed $1.4 billion in assets, according to a Forbes Best-in-State advisor ranking. Sheets and Green are joined by vice presidents and private advisors Nick Routzahn, Hayden Kerns and Cameron Sheets, Chris’s son. Karoline Humphries is serving as the team chief operating officer, while McKenna Whitney has joined as a client associate and analyst. Chris Sheets specializes in alternative and private investments, as well as wealth structuring and pre-liquidity event planning. Green brings expertise in complex planning, including intergenerational wealth transfer, concentrated stock positions, preparing privately held businesses for sale, and generating cash flow. Prior to joining J.P. Morgan in 2018, the team was with Bernstein Private Wealth Management. Rockefeller opened its first office on the west coast of Florida earlier this year. Rockefeller Capital Management began as the family office of John D. Rockefeller in 1882 and was restructured as an independent advisory firm in 2018. The company has since grown to include three distinct businesses—Rockefeller Global Family Office, Rockefeller Global Investment Management and Rockefeller Global Investment Banking. The firm has many locations across the U.S. and one in London, overseeing about $237 billion in client assets. title: JP Morgan: investment surges and inflation bring volatility but family offices are enjoying the ride - Spear's Magazine
content:
The bank's family office co-head has said that 'many feel strongly that the risk of staying out is higher than the risk of getting in' Family offices are increasing their exposure to investment surges in AI and alternatives, appearing unphased by market volatility, according to analysis from JP Morgan. In London last week, JP Morgan held the launch of its Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMAs). The annual briefing, now in its 31st year, is closely watched by the bank’s family office clients, and provides a 10 to 15-year forecast for risks and returns across various asset classes. At the briefing, Karen Ward, chief market strategist for EMEA at JP Morgan Asset Management, identified defence, energy and technology as three areas where government and private expenditure is surging: ‘The more chaotic the world becomes, the more this spending has to happen.’ [See also: Alternative assets now form the majority of family office portfolios] In the report, JP Morgan forecast total annual US AI capital expenditure to peak at $1.2 trillion in 2030, before declining each year after that, reaching just over $800 billion in 2040. ‘The markets are continually assessing whether it’s found a productive home for capital,’ Ward said, adding that technology creation ‘is the fun part’ for markets, whereas once that technology is deployed, ‘that learning process creates a lot of volatility.’ These large investment increases are changing how family offices are approaching portfolio selection, the bank has found. Public equities topped JP Morgan’s list of where family offices have put fresh capital in the last six months, with 81 per cent of those allocating more to equities naming AI as a priority investment theme. [See also: The best wealth managers for high-net-worth clients] John Bilton, head of strategic research, said inflation was also leading clients to rethink their portfolios, and allocate funds towards alternatives. ‘Alternatives are inflation-proof assets, and offer a good opportunity to diversify. I think manager selection has become more and more important,’ he said. Grace Peters, co-head of investment strategy at JP Morgan’s private bank, agreed: ‘The key notion is that there are greater opportunities to diversify, and greater rewards for doing so.’ [See also: J.P. Morgan: UHNWs should invest in security amid geopolitical tensions] Research by JP Morgan’s private bank found that almost half (43 per cent) of family offices have made fresh allocations to alternatives in the last six months. ‘This reflects a deliberate strategic shift, not routine rebalancing,’ the bank’s family office co-head Natacha Minniti commented of the findings. ‘Despite plenty of risk and noisy news flow, family offices have a risk-on attitude. If you look at their behaviour, investors have increased exposure in public and private equity. Many feel strongly that the risk of staying out is higher than the risk of getting in.’ Alluding to recent bond market unrest at this week’s briefing, Ward said lenders faced an ‘ugly beauty contest’ on who to issue debt to: ‘There is much more choice about who to allocate to, and so the bond market has the all-powerful role of having other options,’ she said, adding that southern Europe ‘is in a much more sustainable place’ than it has been for a while. title: Will JPMorgan's Nigeria Expansion Bolster Its Growth Prospects? - TradingView
content: JPMorgan Chase & Co. JPM is advancing its expansion plans in Nigeria after the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) granted approval-in-principle to establish JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited. The move marks a significant step in JPMorgan’s efforts to deepen its presence in Africa’s largest economy and expand its corporate and institutional banking services. Can JPMorgan’s Nigeria Banking License Strengthen Its African Presence? The CBN granted approval-in-principle to JPMorgan on Oct. 23, 2026, allowing it to proceed with plans to establish a merchant bank in Nigeria. The development follows the bank’s reported deposit of 50 billion Nigerian naira (approximately $38 million) with CBN as part of its licensing process. The deposit represented a key regulatory requirement but did not guarantee approval. JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited is expected to expand the bank’s ability to serve Nigerian corporations and institutional clients. Its proposed activities include wholesale banking, capital markets and advisory services. The expansion could also create opportunities in lending, payments, trade finance and cross-border transactions. JPMorgan has maintained a representative office in Lagos for years. Establishing a locally licensed merchant bank would provide a broader platform to serve businesses and participate in Nigeria’s financial markets. The approval-in-principle represents only the initial stage of the regulatory process. JPMorgan Merchant Bank Nigeria Limited must complete the remaining requirements, including incorporation with the Corporate Affairs Commission and the necessary operational arrangements, before receiving authorization to commence business. The proposed Nigerian merchant bank also aligns with JPMorgan’s broader efforts to strengthen its African presence and capture corporate and investment banking opportunities across the region. The bank has reinforced its regional investment banking leadership through appointments covering sub-Saharan Africa, Kenya and Ivory Coast, reflecting its focus on expanding client coverage and strengthening relationships with businesses, governments and institutional investors. Nigeria’s position as a major African economy could make the proposed bank a valuable addition to JPMorgan’s regional operations. However, the scale of the opportunity will depend on regulatory approvals, client demand and the bank’s ability to establish profitable operations. In conclusion, JPMorgan’s planned entry into Nigeria’s merchant banking sector could strengthen its African presence and create new growth opportunities in corporate banking, capital markets, advisory services and cross-border financing. Nigeria’s sizable economy and growing demand for institutional financial services offer significant long-term potential. However, the expansion’s success will depend on securing final regulatory approval, attracting corporate clients and building profitable operations amid competition and market challenges. While the approval-in-principle marks an important milestone, its contribution to JPMorgan’s overall growth will ultimately depend on how effectively the bank converts its expanded presence into sustainable revenue and earnings. title: UDR’s Apollo union is a ‘positive’: J.P. Morgan - Multifamily Dive
content:
