The REIT will earn an asset management fee equaling 1.25% of Apollo’s equity, or $16.75 million, according to Executive Director Anthony Paolone. UDR’s $2 billion joint venture with Apollo got generally good reviews from Wall Street analysts after it was announced last week. Anthony Paolone, executive director at J.P. Morgan, called the JV “positive, in our view, and important, given that cap rates are likely 25bps or more higher today.” In the deal, Apollo-managed funds and affiliates will invest $1.34 billion of capital, acquiring an approximate two-thirds interest in the 19 properties that total 7,059 units. UDR, which will retain a one-third interest, will continue to operate and manage the portfolio and earn an asset management fee equaling 1.25% of Apollo’s equity, or $16.75 million, Paolone said in a research note. The deal seems to accomplish multiple goals for UDR, including lowering the average age of its portfolio, generating liquidity for new deals and stock buybacks and boosting fee-management returns. However, Apollo is a sophisticated operator and there are many unknowns, according to Paolone. In generating liquidity, UDR is trading out of older assets with the JV. The 19 properties, which carry a 6% cap rate, have average revenue per unit of $2,058 and an age of 39 years, per the release from UDR. By comparison, in the second quarter of 2026, UDR’s average rent was $2,642 for its 2Q26 same-store portfolio, Michael Lewis, an analyst for Truist, said in a report shared with Multifamily Dive. Removing the older assets enhances UDR’s “remaining same-store NOI growth rate,” Paolone wrote. The deal also shows that the jump in 10-year Treasury yields may be affecting valuations. “The quoted 6.0% cap rate appears to signal apartment cap rates may have moved up amid the recent spike in interest rates, though it is below the 6.4% implied cap rate on UDR’s stock,” Lewis wrote. Piper Sandler analyst Alexander Goldfarb concurred, writing that the valuations “are beginning to reflect the 5%-handle 10-Year,” with a 6% forward economic cap rate versus a net asset value cap rate of about 5%, he said in a report shared with Multifamily Dive. By comparison, Independence Realty Trust acquired Centerspace at 6.8%, which shows “the cash flow disconnect between the Midwest and Coastal/Sunbelt,” he wrote. Keep up with the story. Subscribe to the Multifamily Dive free daily newsletter With the transaction, UDR will gain “access to a new, low-cost permanent source of equity capital,” CFO Dave Bragg said in the release. The REIT expects to deploy the proceeds into high-growth assets and other general corporate purposes. “The JV provides significant capital to improve/de-lever the balance sheet and pursue new investments,” Lewis said. Paolone said that UDR management expects to use the proceeds for acquisitions in the 5.25% to 5.5% cap rate range, debt paydowns and stock buybacks. He also noted that REITs in other sectors, like Realty Income in net lease, have tapped capital through JVs. “The fees and structure provide UDR with low-cost capital, though with some added complexity and some unknowns around the long-term features of the deal,” Paolone said. “It should be about 1% accretive to the bottom line, which is helpful in a low-growth area like multifamily right now.” Paolone said UDR’s management fee was “sizable” and set the deal apart. With a 6% cap, the $2 billion portfolio would generate about $120 million in net operating income. He said the venture appears to deduct $16.75 million in management fees, pay for capital expenditures and then make a distribution. With a modest capital ex of $10 million, the cash flow for partners would be $93.25 million, according to Paolone. Paolone projects Apollo to receive $62.5 million, or a 4.7% cash return on its investment, while UDR will earn $30.8 million in distributions plus its management fees for a total of $47.5 million. The REIT should be able to produce at least a 5.5% return, or $71.5 million. UDR’s total cash coming in from the deal should be $119 million, compared to $110 million from its wholly owned assets. “Our understanding of how these insurance company deals work is that each party receives pro rata distributions of cash flow,” Paolone wrote. At the fifth anniversary of closing, UDR will have the option to repurchase Apollo’s interest in the JV. While the deal looks like a winner for UDR, Paolone admitted there “could be devils in the details.” “Apollo is a sophisticated counterparty, and we find it hard to believe it is doing these deals in a manner that is completely favorable to the other party,” Paolone said. It’s also unclear what “downside support” UDR is providing to Apollo. “In the few deals we’ve seen REITs do with insurance companies, the finer points have not been disclosed,” he wrote. “This is something we’ll have to watch over time, and it does add complexity, of which we are not a fan.” Still, “on net” the deal looks good for UDR, according to Paolone. “It sheds lower-quality assets at a price level that seems to have been set a few months ago,” he wrote. “It will collect fees and add to earnings. title: J.P. Morgan Projects a 7.0% Annual Return for a 60/40 Investment Portfolio over 10–15 Years - Funds Society
content: The projected annual return for a U.S. dollar-denominated 60/40 stock and bond portfolio over the next 10–15 years rises to 7.0%, although higher correlations between stocks and bonds call for additional diversification. This is the main takeaway from the 31st edition of the 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMA) report by J.P. Morgan Asset Management. The study offers a comprehensive 10- to 15-year outlook on the future returns and risks across various investment asset classes, against a backdrop where inflation uncertainty and market volatility remain elevated. While labor and demographic headwinds may constrain long-term growth potential, the report argues that increased capital expenditure and the adoption of artificial intelligence across sectors will bolster near-term earnings and lift long-term productivity. The report emphasizes the potential of regional equity diversification and the inclusion of alternative assets, particularly hedge funds and real assets. A 60/40+ portfolio with a 30% allocation to diversified alternatives could boost expected returns up to 7.5% and improve the Sharpe ratio by 21% compared to a conventional 60/40 portfolio. “Our long-term capital market assumptions help investors navigate markets reshaped by economic nationalism, technological acceleration, and shifting capital flows. This year’s outlook points to stronger long-term growth and new opportunities to build more resilient portfolios through diversification—combining higher global fixed-income yields with alternative and real assets that deliver differentiated return sources and enhanced inflation protection,” noted John Bilton, Global Head of Multi-Asset Strategy at J.P. Morgan Asset Management. For his part, David Kelly, Chief Global Strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, commented: “The global economy is entering a dynamic investment cycle in which AI adoption and productivity gains reinforce growth prospects. At the same time, demographic challenges, elevated public deficits, and a more complex geopolitical landscape suggest that inflation will remain more volatile across our forecast horizon.” Regarding the report’s practical utility, Grace Peters, Global Co-Head of Investment Strategy at J.P. Morgan Private Bank, explained: “Each year, the assumptions from our LTCMA report provide the foundation for building client portfolios, and that has never been more critical than it is today. Returns matter, but they are no longer the only factor to consider. In the current environment, achieving an optimal balance between risk and return is essential. High market dispersion creates opportunities for investors who take a disciplined approach to strategic asset allocation, looking beyond what the headlines might suggest.” The firm explains that three core forces are shaping the future and will drive returns. The first is economic nationalism, which spurs state investment, though risks linked to inflation volatility persist. Second, technology adoption is underpinning the global economy by driving investment and productivity. Meanwhile, a surge in domestic investment is prompting a reallocation of capital and altering the dynamics of public and private flows. The best growth prospects for the developed world in 15 years: The report notes that a global investment boom focused on artificial intelligence, set to extend through 2040, will lift total factor productivity by 50% to 120 basis points. This boost raises the forecast for U.S. real GDP growth to 2.1% and developed-market nominal growth to 4.2%. In addition, the policy mix of GDP and inflation is the most favorable seen since the pandemic. Furthermore, upward revisions to U.S. equities, a global bond revival, and a maiden analysis of bitcoin take center stage. According to the study, profit margins exceeding 15% lift the forecast for U.S. large-cap equities by 80 basis points to 7.5%, leading developed market equity expectations to surpass emerging markets for the first time in the report’s history. Meanwhile, rising real yields push global aggregate bond forecasts up from a low of 2.1% in 2021 to 5.3% today—the highest level in two decades. The document also includes an expected return range for bitcoin, although the asset is not included as a portfolio allocation. Regarding alternative assets, they offer superior returns, enhanced diversification, and strengthened inflation protection. Higher inflation volatility, persistent currency debasement risks, and expanding alpha-generation opportunities reinforce the role of alternative assets as an indispensable portfolio component and return engine. The analysis lifts the outlook for diversified hedge funds by 140 basis points, supported by sustained alpha resilience and a higher interest-rate regime. Concurrently, it maintains a constructive outlook on real assets given their capacity to hedge against heightened inflation volatility. Intermediate-term U.S. Treasuries are expected to deliver a 4.6% return, supported by expectations of higher policy rates and the reconstitution of term premia, which brightens long-term return prospects. U.S. investment-grade corporate debt is projected to return 6.1%, while U.S. high-yield debt is forecast at 6.7%, with a fair value spread of 440 basis points, driven by improved credit quality among the index’s constituents. U.S. large-cap equities are expected to yield 7.5% (up from 6.7% previously), reflecting persistent technology adoption and productivity gains. Nevertheless, elevated starting valuations and concentration risk remain vital considerations. Globally, equities are projected to return 7.5% (in USD), with non-U.S. markets offering richer diversification potential and benefiting from a U.S. dollar depreciation that proceeds at a more measured pace. For emerging markets, the report projects equity returns of 7.1% (in USD)—a lower figure than the previous year, as AI tailwinds and capital expenditures (capex) normalize. Alternatives encompass several distinct categories: Private Equity: Projected return stands at 9.8%, marking a slight moderation. Return potential remains anchored to consistent value creation and operational efficiencies, including AI integration across portfolio companies. Real Estate: Core U.S. real estate is projected to return 8.1%, while European core real estate is set at 7.1%. Core Global Infrastructure: Forecast to deliver 7.1% (up from 6.5% last year), mirroring supply chain reconfigurations. Commodities: Broad-basket commodities return forecasts rise to 4.8%, as access to critical minerals remains constrained and geopolitical risks weigh on the outlook. Gold holds steady at 5.5%. Timberland: Global timberland assets are expected to generate 6.2%, slightly below the 6.3% recorded the previous year. Hedge Funds: Diversified hedge funds are projected to return 6.7%, up from 5.3% last year, reflecting higher alpha estimates. The Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions (LTCMA) report is the product of an exhaustive research process combining quantitative and qualitative inputs from more than 90 leading portfolio managers, economists, and research analysts globally. These time-tested projections cover over 200 assets denominated in more than 20 currencies, serving as a benchmark for strategic asset allocation and long-term investment planning across today’s evolving financial landscape.

title: JPMorgan Has Nearly $900 Million in Tokenized Funds on Ethereum and Solana. Which Chain Benefits More? - 24/7 Wall St.
content:
JPMorgan just parked nearly $900 million in tokenized funds across Ethereum and Solana, but the fine print reveals one chain got a much bigger piece of the deal than the headlines suggest. It sounds nuts, but SoFi is giving new Active Invest users up to $1,000 in stock for a limited time, and all it takes is a $50 deposit to get started. See for yourself (Sponsor) This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM | JPM Price Prediction) has made headlines by placing nearly $900 million in tokenized funds on both Ethereum (CRYPTO: ETH) and Solana (CRYPTO: SOL). A tokenized fund is an investment fund whose shares exist as tokens on a blockchain, allowing them to trade around the clock. According to Sentora data, the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund (JLTXX) holds about $792 million across both networks, while the My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) holds an estimated $103.1 million on Ethereum alone. In just one week, JPMorgan took two significant steps. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank’s blockchain unit, introduced its JPM Coin deposit token (JPMD) to Ethereum. Shortly after, on October 22, J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched MONY and JLTXX on Solana. However, despite these announcements, both cryptocurrencies saw declines: ETH fell to $2,333, down 2.1% for the week, while SOL dropped to $101, down 1.5%. JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund that invests cash in short-term government debt and passes interest earnings directly to investors. JPMorgan designed it so that stablecoin issuers can hold reserves in JLTXX tokens under the GENIUS Act, a federal stablecoin law. JPMorgan first launched JLTXX on Ethereum in May. MONY, by contrast, is a private placement regulated under the SEC’s Rule 506(c), meaning only high-net-worth individuals can invest. JPMorgan rolled this fund out in December 2025. Both funds operate through Morgan Money, JPMorgan’s cash management platform, allowing investors to subscribe and redeem, then receive tokens at a designated blockchain address. Retail traders cannot purchase these tokens on exchanges. Meanwhile, JPMD is a deposit token representing a dollar held in a JPMorgan bank account, enabling institutional clients to transact at any time. It initially launched on Base, the blockchain connected to Coinbase (NASDAQ: COIN), where Sentora reports a $1 million supply, but it is not yet available on Ethereum. These tokenized funds bring in modest revenue compared to JPMorgan’s core businesses. Fees from these funds contribute to Asset & Wealth Management, which manages over $5.1 trillion in client assets, while payments revenue, including JPMD, grew 12% in the second quarter. Additionally, neither Sentora nor JPMorgan has disclosed how JLTXX’s $792 million is split between Ethereum and Solana, making it hard to say Solana has a significant share. The announcements did not commit anyone to buy or hold ETH or SOL. When a tokenized fund moves its assets, it incurs small transaction fees known as gas. However, money market fund tokens mainly sit in a few institutional wallets, so they generate far less fee activity than stablecoin transfers or trading. The Solana announcement notably excluded details about the on-chain cash used to trade the fund tokens. It mentioned Morgan Money as the subscription channel but did not reference any stablecoin or JPMD for Solana. Until JPMorgan identifies an on-chain cash option for Solana, the bank’s own dollars will remain absent from that chain. When explaining its choice of Ethereum, JPMorgan cited its “established depth of on-chain liquidity and tokenized assets,” yet Sentora still shows no JPMD supply on Ethereum. Paul Przybylski, who leads digital and tokenized assets at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said clients operate across multiple networks, so their liquidity should reflect that need. However, he did not provide specific figures to back that demand. JPMorgan’s timing on Solana also could be considered late, as competitors like BlackRock (NYSE: BLK) and Franklin Templeton introduced tokenized funds there in 2025. Currently, the market appears to be contracting, with Sentora reporting $14.4 billion in tokenized Treasury and money market products across 119 offerings, a 3.5% decline over the past month. Ethereum currently leads JPMorgan’s tokenized funds. MONY’s $103.1 million is entirely Ethereum-based, JLTXX launched there first, and JPMD integrated into Ethereum before any other chain besides Base. Because Base is an Ethereum layer-2 network, the $1 million JPMD supply also links back to Ethereum. JPMorgan and the respective coins gain different advantages from this move. JPMorgan stands to benefit from fee-generating fund assets and a reserve product tailored for stablecoin issuers, while Ethereum and Solana gain enhanced credibility and the potential for increased stablecoin and trading activity stemming from involvement with a prominent bank like JPMorgan. While both networks use a portion of their fees for validator rewards, the flow is negligible at these fund sizes. For now, Ethereum appears to benefit more from JPMorgan’s tokenized funds, though neither asset has guaranteed buyers. ETH has declined 12.5% over the past month, while SOL’s value has fallen 16.1%, trends that far outweigh the impact of a few hundred million dollars in funds. Solana could gain ground if JPMorgan names it as a JPMD network, giving the funds an on-chain cash option there, or if a Solana-based stablecoin issuer starts holding its reserves in JLTXX. If JPMD’s Ethereum supply rises above zero before JPMorgan announces anything for Solana, Ethereum’s lead likely holds, but a Solana JPMD launch first could start shifting the advantage to SOL. A tokenized fund is an investment fund whose shares exist as tokens on a blockchain, allowing them to trade around the clock. According to Sentora data, the JPMorgan OnChain Liquidity-Token Money Market Fund (JLTXX) holds about $792 million across both networks, while the My OnChain Net Yield Fund (MONY) holds an estimated $103.1 million on Ethereum alone. In just one week, JPMorgan took two significant steps. On October 19, 2026, Kinexys, the bank's blockchain unit, introduced its JPM Coin deposit token (JPMD) to Ethereum. Shortly after, on October 22, J.P. Morgan Asset Management launched MONY and JLTXX on Solana. However, despite these announcements, both cryptocurrencies saw declines: ETH fell to $2,333, down 2.1% for the week, while SOL dropped to $101, down 1.5%. JLTXX is a U.S.-registered government money market fund that invests cash in short-term government debt and passes interest earnings directly to investors. Both funds operate through Morgan Money, JPMorgan's cash management platform, allowing investors to subscribe and redeem, then receive tokens at a designated blockchain address. Retail traders cannot purchase these tokens on exchanges. Meanwhile, JPMD is a deposit token representing a dollar held in a JPMorgan bank account, enabling institutional clients to transact at any time. It initially launched on Base, the blockchain connected to Coinbase (NASDAQ: COIN), where Sentora reports a $1 million supply, but it is not yet available on Ethereum. Paul Przybylski, who leads digital and tokenized assets at J.P. Morgan Asset Management, said clients operate across multiple networks, so their liquidity should reflect that need. However, he did not provide specific figures to back that demand. JPMorgan's timing on Solana also could be considered late, as competitors like BlackRock (NYSE: BLK) and Franklin Templeton introduced tokenized funds there in 2025. Solana could gain ground if JPMorgan names it as a JPMD network, giving the funds an on-chain cash option there, or if a Solana-based stablecoin issuer starts holding its reserves in JLTXX. If JPMD's Ethereum supply rises above zero before JPMorgan announces anything for Solana, Ethereum's lead likely holds, but a Solana JPMD launch first could start shifting the advantage to SOL.
